summary: Defines the BGP Tunnel Encapsulation attribute, which can accompany BGP updates to supply the information needed to create tunnels and their headers. It provides encodings for many tunnel types, along with procedures for choosing among alternatives.

plainLanguage.summary: A Border Gateway Protocol (BGP) route can include instructions for sending traffic through a tunnel. Those instructions identify the tunnel endpoint and can provide values needed to build its header.

what is the tunnel egress endpoint sub-tlv
subtitle: How BGP routes can carry tunnel types, endpoints, and encapsulation details for forwarding packets.

tldr.problem: A router may need to tunnel a packet to a BGP next hop, but it needs the tunnel type, endpoint, and header values to do so.
tldr.mechanism: The optional transitive Tunnel Encapsulation path attribute carries tunnel TLVs and sub-TLVs with endpoint addresses, encapsulation fields, and tunnel-selection information.
tldr.outcome: RFC 9012 obsoletes RFC 5512 and RFC 5566, updates RFC 5640, and is itself updated by RFC 9830.

today: RFC 9012 is a Proposed Standard that obsoletes RFC 5512 and RFC 5566, and updates RFC 5640. It is updated by RFC 9830.

sections.title: Why Routes Need Tunnel Information
sections.content:
A router can have a route whose BGP next hop is reachable, even when the routers along the way do not know the packet's final destination. In that case, the packet can be encapsulated and sent through a tunnel to the next hop. The sending router needs to know which tunnel type to use and what values to put in its headers.

RFC 9012 replaces RFC 5512, whose attribute was limited to the Encapsulation SAFI and did not provide a general way to signal the tunnel egress address or outer-header values. RFC 9012 lets BGP updates for specified address families carry this information alongside routes.
sections.plainLanguage: When intermediate routers cannot route a packet directly, it can travel inside a tunnel to a known router. The route can carry instructions for building that tunnel.

sections.title: Tunnel TLVs and Sub-TLVs
sections.content:
The Tunnel Encapsulation attribute is an optional transitive BGP path attribute with type code 23. It contains one or more TLVs. Each Tunnel TLV identifies a tunnel type and contains sub-TLVs that provide details for that tunnel. The tunnel type and length are each 2 octets.

A sub-TLV has a type, a length, and a value. Types from 0 to 127 use a 1-octet length; types from 128 to 255 use a 2-octet length. TLV order has no significance, and multiple TLVs of the same tunnel type describe separate tunnel choices.
sections.plainLanguage: The BGP attribute is a container for tunnel descriptions. Each description can include smaller fields with the endpoint and header information.

sections.title: Tunnel Endpoints and Header Details
sections.content:
The Tunnel Egress Endpoint sub-TLV (type 6) identifies the router that removes the tunnel encapsulation. It can carry an IPv4 or IPv6 address; address family 0 means to use the route's BGP next hop. In the address families covered by the RFC, every tunnel TLV must contain exactly one egress endpoint sub-TLV.

Encapsulation sub-TLVs provide tunnel-specific values. The RFC defines formats for VXLAN, NVGRE, L2TPv3, GRE, and MPLS-in-GRE. Other sub-TLVs can specify the outer DS field or UDP destination port, restrict the payload protocol, match a tunnel by color, control an embedded MPLS label, provide an MPLS label stack, or carry a Prefix-SID value.

The earlier Encapsulation Extended Community remains for a limited, barebones tunnel description. When such a description is sufficient, the RFC requires using the extended community, while implementations must still process a matching barebones TLV.
sections.plainLanguage: One field says where the tunnel ends. Other fields can supply values for the tunnel header or limit which packets can use it.

sections.title: Selecting and Using a Tunnel
sections.content:
A tunnel is feasible only if the router supports its type, it can carry the packet, its endpoint is reachable, and local policy allows it. If at least one feasible tunnel is listed, the router sends the packet through one of them. Local policy may choose among several options, using color or protocol-type information as appropriate.

If no tunnel is feasible, the route is not considered resolvable for BGP route selection. When next-hop resolution leads to another route carrying a Tunnel Encapsulation attribute, the packet must use a feasible tunnel from that route. Tunnels can be stacked when the route to one tunnel endpoint has its own tunnel instructions.

For VXLAN and NVGRE, the RFC defines how a virtual network identifier and any label embedded in a labeled NLRI are selected or carried. If required values are unavailable, the tunnel cannot be used.
sections.plainLanguage: The router checks which advertised tunnels can carry the packet and reach their endpoint. It uses a permitted tunnel, or treats the route as unusable if none qualifies.

sections.title: Handling Unknown and Malformed Information
sections.content:
A malformed attribute, including one with no valid TLVs or a TLV whose length does not end at its final sub-TLV, uses BGP's treat-as-withdraw procedure. An unknown tunnel type is treated as absent, but remains in the attribute if the route is propagated. Unknown sub-TLVs are handled similarly.

Most sub-TLV types must not appear more than once; later duplicates are disregarded. A malformed egress endpoint is different: the entire containing Tunnel TLV is ignored and removed before the route is distributed. A valid but unreachable endpoint is not malformed; it simply makes that tunnel infeasible.
sections.plainLanguage: A router can ignore fields it does not recognize and keep them when forwarding the route. A bad tunnel endpoint causes the router to discard that tunnel description.

sections.title: Scope, Routing, and Security
sections.content:
The attribute must stay within a well-defined administrative scope. Routers that understand it must be able to filter it on incoming and outgoing updates; filtering must be enabled by default on external BGP sessions. The same scoping rules apply to the Encapsulation Extended Community.

A malicious or incorrect endpoint can divert traffic, potentially enabling traffic inspection, modification, or denial of service. The RFC describes an optional check that compares the endpoint's originating AS with the route origin, but notes that this does not guarantee safety. Operators should also avoid mutually recursive tunnel dependencies and account for reduced MTU when tunnels are stacked.
sections.plainLanguage: Tunnel instructions should only travel within the intended routing scope. Incorrect or hostile instructions can redirect traffic, so routers need filtering and operators need to avoid tunnel loops.
